questions.clue: A parameter multiplies a predictor term in the model equation.
questions.explanation: Its role is to quantify how that term contributes to the fitted response or link scale.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 362, Regression coefficient

questions.clue: An observed response minus the corresponding fitted response.
questions.explanation: It measures the fitted model's error for a particular observation.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 367, Residual

questions.clue: The model's estimated response evaluated at a training observation's predictor values.
questions.explanation: The fitted value is the model's prediction at that design point.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 367, Residual

questions.clue: The relationship between one predictor and the response changes with another predictor.
questions.explanation: A product term is one way to let the effect of a predictor depend on another variable.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 219, Interaction

questions.clue: A model uses 1 for the afternoon shift and 0 for the morning shift.
questions.explanation: A zero-one indicator represents membership in the selected group.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 145, Dummy variables

questions.clue: Separate fitted lines show that sales rise faster with advertising in one region than another.
questions.explanation: An advertising-by-region term allows different slopes by region.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 219, Interaction

questions.clue: Holding the other predictors fixed, the fitted response rises by 2 units per extra machine hour.
questions.explanation: The slope coefficient gives the change associated with a one-unit predictor increase.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 362, Regression coefficient

questions.clue: At a design point with fitted value 10, an observation is 13. What is the observed-minus-fitted discrepancy called?
questions.explanation: Subtract the fitted response from the observed response to obtain the residual.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 367, Residual

questions.clue: 1 − SSE / SST, for ordinary least squares with an intercept
questions.explanation: This is the fraction of total variation accounted for by the fitted regression.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 89, Coefficient of determination
questions.convention: SSE is the residual sum of squares. SST is the centred total sum of squares.
questions.math_clue:
$1-\frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{\mathrm{SST}}$
For ordinary least squares with an intercept.

questions.clue: Σᵢ (yᵢ − ŷᵢ)²
questions.explanation: It totals the squared distances between observed and fitted responses.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 368, Residual sum of squares
questions.math_clue: $\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2$

questions.clue: SSE / (n − p), with p fitted coefficients including the intercept
questions.explanation: Dividing the residual sum by residual degrees of freedom estimates the error variance in the classical linear model.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 153, Error mean square
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{\mathrm{SSE}}{n-p}$
Here p is the number of fitted coefficients including the intercept.

questions.clue: MS for a model term / MS for error, in a standard one-factor ANOVA
questions.explanation: The ratio is the F statistic for the term in this ANOVA.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 274, Mean square ratio
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{\mathrm{MS\ for\ a\ model\ term}}{\mathrm{MS\ for\ error}}$
In a standard one-factor ANOVA.

questions.clue: A categorical explanatory variable whose categories define the groups being compared in ANOVA.
questions.explanation: Each category is a level of the factor.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 161, Factor

questions.clue: A linear combination of group means with coefficients that sum to zero.
questions.explanation: The coefficients specify the comparison while cancelling a common shift in all means.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 103, Contrast

questions.clue: A term whose levels are the particular settings of interest, with separate parameters for them.
questions.explanation: A fixed-effects model treats differences among those settings as parameters.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 169, Fixed effects

questions.clue: A group-specific departure modeled as a draw from a distribution of such departures.
questions.explanation: The model learns about variation across groups through a common distribution.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 354, Random effects

questions.clue: Compare the mean yield across three fertilisers with one grouping variable.
questions.explanation: A single factor defines the fertiliser groups whose means are compared.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 13, Analysis of variance (ANOVA)

questions.clue: Compare mean yield by fertiliser and irrigation category, allowing the fertiliser effect to differ by irrigation.
questions.explanation: Two factors and their interaction describe the group mean structure.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 13, Analysis of variance (ANOVA); 161, Factorial designs

questions.clue: Compare mean yield across fertilisers while adjusting for a numerical measure of initial soil quality.
questions.explanation: ANCOVA combines a group comparison with adjustment for a covariate.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 13, Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA)

questions.clue: Divide fields by soil type, then randomly assign the fertilisers within each soil type.
questions.explanation: Randomisation within blocks separates treatment contrasts from block differences.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 58, Blocking

questions.clue: Every combination of two processing temperatures and three mixing speeds is included in the experiment.
questions.explanation: Crossing the factor levels lets the analyst study main effects and interactions.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 161, Factorial designs

questions.clue: Before collecting data, specify a comparison between the control mean and the average of three treatment means.
questions.explanation: A zero-sum set of weights defines this comparison in advance.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 103, Contrast

questions.clue: Estimate a fixed treatment difference and model a random intercept for each clinic.
questions.explanation: The model includes both fixed parameters and clinic-level random effects.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 205, Linear Models with Random Effects

questions.clue: Choose regression coefficients by minimising the sum of squared prediction errors on the data.
questions.explanation: Least squares minimises the residual sum of squares.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 245, Least squares estimation

questions.clue: Hospital type forms the rows and discharge status the columns, with patient counts in the cells.
questions.explanation: A contingency table cross-classifies observations on categorical variables.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 101, Contingency tables

questions.clue: Test independence in a sparse 2 × 2 table using exact probabilities conditional on its margins.
questions.explanation: The exact test avoids relying on a large-sample chi-square approximation.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 167, Fisher’s exact test

questions.clue: Compare yes/no responses before and after treatment on the same patients using the discordant pairs.
questions.explanation: McNemar's test looks for an imbalance between the two kinds of discordance.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 274, McNemar’s test

questions.clue: With adequate cell counts, test independence by summing squared observed-minus-expected counts divided by expected counts.
questions.explanation: The test compares actual cell counts with those expected under independence.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 323, Pearson’s chi-squared statistic

questions.clue: ad / bc for the table with rows (a, b) and (c, d)
questions.explanation: Cross multiplication gives the ratio of the two row odds for a positive-cell table.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 309, Odds ratio
questions.convention: Column one is the event in both rows.
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{ad}{bc}$
For the table with rows (a, b) and (c, d).

questions.clue: [a / (a + b)] ÷ [c / (c + d)] for rows (a, b) and (c, d)
questions.explanation: Divide the event proportion in the first row by that in the second row.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 364, Relative risk
questions.convention: Column one is the event in both rows.
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{a/(a+b)}{c/(c+d)}$
For the table with rows (a, b) and (c, d).

questions.clue: ln[p / (1 − p)] for 0 < p < 1
questions.explanation: The logit converts a probability to the natural logarithm of its odds.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 258, Logit
questions.math_clue:
$\ln\left[\frac{p}{1-p}\right]$
For p strictly between zero and one.

questions.clue: Σ cells (O − E)² / E, with E > 0
questions.explanation: Each cell contributes its squared count discrepancy scaled by its expected count.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 323, Pearson’s chi-squared statistic
questions.math_clue:
$\sum_{\mathrm{cells}}\frac{(O-E)^2}{E}$
For positive expected counts E.

questions.clue: Some predictors are nearly linear combinations of other predictors.
questions.explanation: It can make the separate coefficient estimates imprecise even if predictions remain stable.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 287, Multicollinearity

questions.clue: The conditional error variance changes across predictor values.
questions.explanation: A changing error spread violates the constant-variance assumption.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 204, Heteroscedasticity

questions.clue: The variability exceeds what the fitted Poisson or binomial model allows.
questions.explanation: An extra source of variability can make standard errors from the original model too small.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 314, Overdispersion

questions.clue: An observation lies unusually far from the centre of the predictor design.
questions.explanation: High leverage comes from unusual predictor values and can occur with a small residual.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 247, Leverage points

questions.clue: An analyst wants one index for how much the whole fitted regression shifts after removing a case.
questions.explanation: Cook’s distance summarizes a case’s influence on the fitted model.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 104, Cook’s distance

questions.clue: An analyst wants the deletion effect on one particular regression coefficient.
questions.explanation: DFBETA isolates the change in a particular coefficient when an observation is removed.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 132, DFBETA

questions.clue: After adding correlated predictors, an analyst measures how much less precisely one slope is estimated.
questions.explanation: The VIF links the slope’s inflated variance to its predictor’s relationship with the other predictors.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 445, Variance inflation factor

questions.clue: An analyst compares ordered residuals with expected normal quantiles to inspect the distributional assumption.
questions.explanation: Systematic departures from a straight line indicate departures from a normal shape.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 339, Probability plot

questions.clue: 1 / (1 − Rⱼ²), using the regression of predictor j on the other predictors
questions.explanation: A larger auxiliary R² means greater inflation of the coefficient’s variance.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 445, Variance inflation factor
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{1}{1-R_j^2}$
Use the regression of predictor j on the other predictors.

questions.clue: hᵢᵢ, the ith diagonal entry of X(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ
questions.explanation: The diagonal weight measures how strongly an observation’s response enters its own fitted value.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 247, Leverage points
questions.math_clue:
$X(X^\mathrm{T}X)^{-1}X^\mathrm{T}$
Identify hᵢᵢ, the ith diagonal entry of this matrix.

questions.clue: (eᵢ² / p MSE) × hᵢᵢ / (1 − hᵢᵢ)² in ordinary least squares
questions.explanation: A large residual and high leverage can combine to give a case substantial influence.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 104, Cook’s distance
questions.convention: p includes the intercept, and MSE is the full-model residual mean square.
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{e_i^2}{p\,\mathrm{MSE}}\times\frac{h_{ii}}{(1-h_{ii})^2}$
In ordinary least squares.

questions.clue: eᵢ / [s₍ᵢ₎ √(1 − hᵢᵢ)], with s₍ᵢ₎ estimated after deleting case i
questions.explanation: The deleted-case variance estimate keeps the tested observation out of the scale estimate.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 419, Studentized residual
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{e_i}{s_{(i)}\sqrt{1-h_{ii}}}$
The scale s₍ᵢ₎ is estimated after deleting case i.

questions.clue: The outcome modeled as a function of other variables.
questions.explanation: The regression equation predicts or describes this variable.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 369, Response variable

questions.clue: An input used to explain or predict changes in a modeled outcome.
questions.explanation: This variable is used on the predictor side of the model.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 157, Explanatory variables

questions.clue: The fitted linear predictor when every numerical predictor equals zero and factors are at their reference levels.
questions.explanation: The intercept is the constant term in the model equation.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 253, Linear model

questions.clue: The parameter attached to a particular basis term of a regression equation.
questions.explanation: The coefficient determines the contribution of its associated term.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 362, Regression coefficient

questions.clue: A continuous outcome is fitted using additive linear terms for floor area, age and distance.
questions.explanation: The model has more than one explanatory variable in a linear equation for the mean.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 291, Multiple linear regression

questions.clue: A curve for a continuous outcome includes both x and x squared as predictors.
questions.explanation: Powers of the predictor let a model linear in its coefficients fit a curved relationship.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 331, Polynomial regression

questions.clue: Fit a straight line by minimizing squared errors multiplied by known positive precision weights.
questions.explanation: The criterion gives lower-variance observations larger weights when weights are inverse variances.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 456, Weighted least squares

questions.clue: A calibration line is required to predict a response of zero when its single input is zero.
questions.explanation: Fixing the intercept at zero forces the fitted line through the origin.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 363, Regression through the origin

questions.clue: bⱼ × SD(xⱼ) / SD(y) for a fitted linear model with an intercept
questions.explanation: This is the slope for predictor j when both the outcome and predictor are put on standard deviation scales.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 410, Standardized regression coefficient
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{b_j\times\mathrm{SD}(x_j)}{\mathrm{SD}(y)}$
For a fitted linear model with an intercept.

questions.clue: corr(eₓ, eᵧ), after regressing both x and y separately on the same controls
questions.explanation: It measures the linear association left after removing the effects of the controls from both variables.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 318, Partial correlation
questions.math_clue:
$\mathrm{corr}(e_x,e_y)$
After regressing both x and y separately on the same controls.

questions.clue: corr(y, ŷ) in a nonconstant least-squares fit with an intercept
questions.explanation: The sample multiple correlation equals the nonnegative square root of R².
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 290, Multiple correlation coefficient
questions.math_clue:
$\mathrm{corr}(y,\hat y)$
In a nonconstant least-squares fit with an intercept.

questions.clue: yᵢ − ŷᵢ for the ith fitted observation
questions.explanation: Subtracting the fitted value from the observation gives the model error for that case.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 367, Residual
questions.math_clue:
$y_i-\hat y_i$
For the ith fitted observation.

questions.clue: Analysis of a continuous outcome using two categorical factors and optionally their interaction.
questions.explanation: Each factor contributes group differences, and the interaction captures departures from additivity.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 13, Analysis of variance (ANOVA); 161, Factorial designs

questions.clue: Analysis testing equality of several group means indexed by a single factor.
questions.explanation: One categorical variable defines the groups.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 13, Analysis of variance (ANOVA)

questions.clue: An experiment randomly assigns treatments separately within each deliberately formed group of experimental units.
questions.explanation: Blocks remove some nuisance variation from comparisons among treatments.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 58, Blocking

questions.clue: A model combines population-level coefficients and subject-specific terms treated as draws from a distribution.
questions.explanation: It represents systematic differences and variation across subjects in one model.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 205, Linear Models with Random Effects

questions.clue: Σᵢ (yᵢ − ȳ)²
questions.explanation: This quantity measures spread about the overall mean before accounting for regressors or treatments.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 432, Total sum of squares
questions.math_clue: $\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2$

questions.clue: 2μ₁ − μ₂ − μ₃, for three group means. The coefficients sum to zero.
questions.explanation: The weights 2, −1 and −1 sum to zero, so a common shift in means cancels out.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 103, Contrast
questions.math_clue:
$2\mu_1-\mu_2-\mu_3$
For three group means. The coefficients sum to zero.

questions.clue: SS for treatment / df for treatment
questions.explanation: An ANOVA mean square scales a sum of squares by its own degrees of freedom.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 274, Mean squares
questions.math_clue: $\frac{\mathrm{SS\ for\ treatment}}{\mathrm{df\ for\ treatment}}$

questions.clue: MS for treatment / MS for error under the ordinary between-groups ANOVA test
questions.explanation: The numerator measures spread attributable to treatment relative to the denominator's error spread.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 176, F-test; 274, Mean square ratio
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{\mathrm{MS\ for\ treatment}}{\mathrm{MS\ for\ error}}$
Under the ordinary between-groups ANOVA test.

questions.clue: To control familywise error at α, test each of six planned hypotheses at α/6.
questions.explanation: The union bound keeps the overall false-positive risk at or below α.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 59, Bonferroni correction
questions.math_clue:
To control familywise error at α across six planned hypotheses, use this cutoff for each test.
$\frac{\alpha}{6}$

questions.clue: An agronomist compares the average response of two active treatments to the response of one control.
questions.explanation: Weights of ½, ½ and −1 express that comparison.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 103, Contrast

questions.clue: A drug improves scores in one age group and lowers them in another.
questions.explanation: Opposite treatment effects indicate a treatment-by-age interaction.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 219, Interaction

questions.clue: Researchers compare only four named office locations, using a separate parameter for each location's difference.
questions.explanation: Fixed location effects directly describe these four locations.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 169, Fixed effects

questions.clue: Model a yes/no outcome by making the log of its odds a linear function of patient age.
questions.explanation: The most common logistic model uses a logit link for a binary outcome.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 257, Logistic regression

questions.clue: Predict the number of arrivals per hour by modeling the log of the expected count.
questions.explanation: A log link keeps fitted Poisson means positive.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 330, Poisson regression

questions.clue: Model a pass/fail outcome by applying the standard normal CDF to a linear predictor.
questions.explanation: The inverse of the normal CDF gives the corresponding link function.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 340, Probit analysis

questions.clue: Fit ordered ratings with a single set of predictor slopes across all cumulative logit cut points.
questions.explanation: The intercept can vary with the threshold while the slopes are shared.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 344, Proportional-odds model

questions.clue: For paired ratings in a square table, the row and column variables have identical marginal distributions.
questions.explanation: Each category has the same overall probability on each measurement occasion.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 267, Marginal homogeneity

questions.clue: In a square table, each off-diagonal cell has the same probability as its transposed cell.
questions.explanation: Swapping the two categorical variables leaves the joint distribution unchanged.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 424, Symmetry in square contingency tables

questions.clue: A test comparing the proportions of successes for three or more matched binary conditions.
questions.explanation: The observations are linked within each experimental unit across conditions.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 88, Cochran’s Q-test

questions.clue: A summary of the common odds ratio across several 2 × 2 strata.
questions.explanation: It combines the within-stratum table information into a common effect estimate.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 266, Mantel–Haenszel estimator

questions.clue: The treatment looks better within both age groups, yet looks worse after the groups are pooled.
questions.explanation: Unequal group weights can reverse the direction of an association after aggregation.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 394, Simpson’s paradox

questions.clue: A report divides the event proportion among exposed patients by the event proportion among unexposed patients.
questions.explanation: This ratio compares event probabilities directly.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 364, Relative risk

questions.clue: Before testing association, a researcher computes row total × column total ÷ grand total for a cell.
questions.explanation: The formula uses the fitted table under row–column independence.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 156, Expected frequencies
questions.math_clue:
Before testing association, a researcher uses this expression for one cell.
$\frac{\mathrm{row\ total}\times\mathrm{column\ total}}{\mathrm{grand\ total}}$

questions.clue: An analyst sums hypergeometric probabilities over tables at least as extreme in a small 2 × 2 test with fixed margins.
questions.explanation: Fixing the margins gives the null probabilities of the possible tables.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 167, Fisher’s exact test

questions.clue: The vertical spread of residuals grows steadily as the fitted values increase.
questions.explanation: A fan shape suggests the conditional error variance is changing.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 204, Heteroscedasticity

questions.clue: Positive residuals tend to be followed by positive residuals in monthly order.
questions.explanation: The error sequence shows dependence across time.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 25, Autocorrelation

questions.clue: Floor area and room count predict each other closely, leaving individual coefficient estimates imprecise.
questions.explanation: Similar predictors make separating their contributions difficult.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 287, Multicollinearity

questions.clue: A fitted observation has predictor values far from those of the other observations but a small residual.
questions.explanation: An unusual predictor profile can have high leverage without a large error.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 247, Leverage points

questions.clue: (O − E) / √E for a cell count where E > 0
questions.explanation: It scales the signed cell discrepancy using the square root of the fitted expected count.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 323, Pearson’s residual
questions.convention: Uses the raw Pearson form without an adjustment for fitted margins.
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{O-E}{\sqrt{E}}$
For a cell count with positive expected value E.

questions.clue: 2 × [log L(saturated model) − log L(fitted model)]
questions.explanation: The log-likelihood gap measures how much fit is lost by using the chosen model.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 131, Deviance
questions.math_clue: $2\times[\log L(\mathrm{saturated\ model})-\log L(\mathrm{fitted\ model})]$

questions.clue: β̂ⱼ − β̂ⱼ₍ᵢ₎, where the second estimate omits observation i
questions.explanation: This measures the observed case's effect on one fitted coefficient.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 132, DFBETA
questions.math_clue:
$\hat{\beta}_j-\hat{\beta}_{j(i)}$
The second estimate omits observation i.

questions.clue: eᵢ / [s √(1 − hᵢᵢ)] with s from the full linear model
questions.explanation: The denominator accounts for both estimated error scale and leverage.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 410, Standardized residual
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{e_i}{s\sqrt{1-h_{ii}}}$
Use s from the full linear model.

questions.clue: A model checker graphs observed-minus-fitted values against the fitted values to look for curvature.
questions.explanation: Curvature can indicate that the fitted mean model misses some systematic pattern.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 367, Residual plots

questions.clue: A model checker compares each ranked residual with the normal score for that rank.
questions.explanation: An approximately straight pattern supports a normal error shape.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 339, Probability plot

questions.clue: A model fitting method limits how far a few very large residuals can pull the estimates.
questions.explanation: Reducing the influence of unusually large errors protects the fit from outliers.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 372, Robust regression

questions.clue: One observed response is far from the fitted value, despite having typical predictor measurements.
questions.explanation: An unusually large residual flags a potential response outlier.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 313, Outlier; 362, Regression diagnostics

questions.clue: In a multiple linear regression, what is a fitted value for one observation?
choices: The model's prediction at that observation's predictors
The difference between observed and predicted responses
The intercept evaluated at every observation
questions.answer: The model's prediction at that observation's predictors
questions.explanation: A fitted value is the response the model predicts for a specified predictor profile.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 362, Regression coefficient

questions.clue: A salary regression includes experience and education. What does the experience coefficient describe?
choices: The fitted salary change when both predictors rise one unit
The fitted education change per unit of salary
The fitted salary change per year of experience at the same education
The mean salary at zero education
The observed salary difference for all workers
questions.answer: The fitted salary change per year of experience at the same education
questions.explanation: Each slope describes a one-unit change in its predictor holding the others fixed.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 362, Regression coefficient

questions.clue: A least-squares prediction of demand is below actual demand. What does this say about the usual residual?
choices: It has the units of a variance
questions.explanation: The usual residual is observed minus fitted, so a prediction below the observation leaves a positive residual.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 367, Residual

questions.clue: A regression uses an indicator for evening shifts, with morning shifts as the reference category. Which term represents the fitted mean in the reference category when this is the only predictor?
choices: The fitted mean across both shifts weighted equally
The standard error of the indicator slope
questions.explanation: The indicator is zero for the reference group and leaves only the intercept.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 145, Dummy variables

questions.clue: In an intercept-plus-indicator regression, what does switching the reference group do to the indicator coefficient?
choices: It turns the fitted group difference into a residual
It leaves its sign unchanged when the group means differ
It replaces the group difference with its square
It adds the grand mean to the original group difference
It reverses the sign of the fitted group difference
questions.answer: It reverses the sign of the fitted group difference
questions.explanation: Reversing the reference reverses the order of subtraction while preserving fitted group means.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 145, Dummy variables

questions.clue: A regression contains a numerical predictor and its interaction with a two-group indicator. Which model feature describes how the numerical predictor's slope differs between groups?
choices: The slope in the reference group alone
questions.explanation: The interaction coefficient measures the slope change from the reference group to the other group.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 219, Interaction

questions.clue: A linear model includes a numerical predictor, a group indicator, and their product. If the product has a nonzero coefficient, how should the fitted difference between groups be described?
choices: It is constant across all predictor values
It depends only on residual variance
It is always equal to the intercept
It is always equal to the product coefficient
It depends on where the numerical predictor is evaluated
questions.answer: It depends on where the numerical predictor is evaluated
questions.explanation: As the numerical predictor changes, the product term changes the gap between the fitted group responses.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 219, Interaction

questions.clue: A model’s only predictor is centred age, which equals zero at age 50. What does the intercept estimate?
choices: The overall mean outcome regardless of the age distribution
The mean fitted outcome at age 50
The mean fitted outcome at age zero
questions.answer: The mean fitted outcome at age 50
questions.explanation: The centred predictor equals zero at age 50.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 253, Linear model

questions.clue: Which residual summary does ordinary least squares minimize when fitting a line?
questions.explanation: Ordinary least squares chooses coefficients that minimize the total of squared observed-minus-fitted differences.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 245, Least squares estimation

questions.clue: What does a positive regression slope mean when the numerical predictor's units are changed from metres to centimetres?
choices: The numerical slope stays the same but changes direction
The fitted direction is determined by the new intercept
The fitted response must be expressed in centimetres
The fitted direction stays positive even though the numerical slope changes
questions.answer: The fitted direction stays positive even though the numerical slope changes
questions.explanation: A positive scaling of the predictor changes the slope's units without reversing the direction of its fitted relationship.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 362, Regression coefficient

questions.clue: Which comparison underlies the coefficient of determination in ordinary least squares with an intercept?
choices: Total variation against variation in one predictor only
Residual variance against the fitted intercept
Mean fitted response against the smallest observed response
Variation in estimated slopes against the sample size
Residual variation against total variation about the response mean
questions.answer: Residual variation against total variation about the response mean
questions.explanation: The coefficient measures the share of total response variation accounted for by the fit.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 89, Coefficient of determination

questions.clue: Add a predictor to an ordinary least-squares model using the same data. What can happen to the minimized residual sum of squares?
choices: It can rise or stay unchanged
It can fall or stay unchanged
questions.answer: It can fall or stay unchanged
questions.explanation: The old fitted values remain achievable by setting the new coefficient to zero.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 368, Residual sum of squares

questions.clue: Why can two equal residuals contribute differently to a weighted least-squares objective?
choices: Their squared residuals are multiplied by different weights
Their squared residuals are sorted by rank before combining
Only their signs determine their contribution
Their response units are always different
Their weights affect only an intercept, never their residuals
questions.answer: Their squared residuals are multiplied by different weights
questions.explanation: The objective adds weighted squared residuals, so differing weights give differing contributions.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 456, Weighted least squares

questions.clue: A team fits a regression line using temperatures from one growing season. Which prediction requires extrapolation?
choices: A temperature above all those used for fitting
The lowest temperature used for fitting
The highest temperature used for fitting
A temperature between two observed values
The average temperature used for fitting
questions.answer: A temperature above all those used for fitting
questions.explanation: Extrapolation applies the fitted relationship outside the observed predictor range.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 159, Extrapolation

questions.clue: A farming trial compares wheat yield at four nitrogen doses. What are the factor's levels?
choices: The plots in each dose group
questions.explanation: The dose is the factor and the four settings are its levels.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 161, Factor

questions.clue: A one-way ANOVA compares mean reading times across three font groups. Which variable is the response?
questions.explanation: The outcome measured for each person is the reading time.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 13, Analysis of variance (ANOVA)

questions.clue: In a one-way ANOVA, what determines the treatment degrees of freedom?
choices: Only the total number of observations
Only the standard deviation within each group
The number of unequal observed responses
The number of independently estimable differences among the group means
The number of treatment observations minus the largest group size
questions.answer: The number of independently estimable differences among the group means
questions.explanation: One overall mean accounts for a common location. Treatment degrees of freedom describe the remaining differences among means.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 13, Analysis of variance (ANOVA)

questions.clue: Why are there fewer residual degrees of freedom than observations in an ordinary one-way ANOVA?
choices: Each group supplies only one observation for the fit
One group is left out entirely
The residuals are sorted by size
A group mean is estimated for each group
The response is replaced by its ranks
questions.answer: A group mean is estimated for each group
questions.explanation: Estimating each group mean uses one degree of freedom.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 13, Analysis of variance (ANOVA)

questions.clue: Which quantities determine the within-group mean square in an ordinary one-way ANOVA?
choices: Treatment sum of squares and residual degrees of freedom
Residual sum of squares and residual degrees of freedom
Residual sum of squares and treatment degrees of freedom
Total sum of squares and treatment degrees of freedom
Treatment mean square and number of blocks
questions.answer: Residual sum of squares and residual degrees of freedom
questions.explanation: The within-group mean square scales the residual sum of squares by its corresponding degrees of freedom.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 274, Mean squares

questions.clue: In a one-way ANOVA, which term measures differences between each fitted group mean and the grand mean, with group sizes used as weights?
questions.explanation: Between-group variation measures how fitted means differ around the overall response mean.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 13, Analysis of variance (ANOVA)

questions.clue: A valid one-way ANOVA rejects equality of four population means. What does this establish at the test's stated significance level?
choices: Evidence that at least one mean differs
Evidence that only the largest mean differs
Evidence of a linear ordering of means
questions.answer: Evidence that at least one mean differs
questions.explanation: The omnibus alternative is that the means are not all equal.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 13, Analysis of variance (ANOVA)

questions.clue: A planned contrast compares a control group with the average of three treatment group means. What does assigning equal weights to the treatment means ensure?
choices: Only the treatment group with the largest sample matters
The treatment groups must have identical observed means
Each treatment group mean enters equally even when group sizes differ
The comparison weights individual observations equally across unequal treatment groups
The control group drops out of the comparison
questions.answer: Each treatment group mean enters equally even when group sizes differ
questions.explanation: Equal contrast weights apply to the group means and give each treatment group equal importance.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 103, Contrast

questions.clue: Why does a contrast of group means remain unchanged when every group mean shifts by the same amount?
choices: Its coefficients are restricted to whole numbers
It uses only the largest group mean
questions.explanation: The common shift enters multiplied by the sum of the coefficients, which is zero.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 103, Contrast

questions.clue: A treatment is tested at two sites. Which comparison specifically targets the interaction between site and treatment?
choices: Compare the treatment-versus-control differences across the sites
Compare the sites after discarding the treatment assignments
Compare all treated observations with the pooled controls only
Compare the spreads in the two control groups
Compare the total sample sizes at the two sites
questions.answer: Compare the treatment-versus-control differences across the sites
questions.explanation: Interaction asks whether the treatment effect changes between sites.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 219, Interaction

questions.clue: In a full two-factor ANOVA, which quantities determine the interaction degrees of freedom?
choices: The residual standard deviations for the two factors
The degrees of freedom for the two factors
The observed size of each main effect
The number of repeated measurements only
questions.answer: The degrees of freedom for the two factors
questions.explanation: The full interaction uses the product of the factor degrees of freedom.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 161, Factorial designs

questions.clue: A test applies all three formulations within each of six labs. Why include lab as a block?
choices: To treat lab as the measured response
To force every lab's results to match
To estimate a fourth formulation mean
To account for baseline differences among labs
questions.answer: To account for baseline differences among labs
questions.explanation: Blocking separates lab-to-lab baseline variation from within-lab formulation comparisons.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 58, Blocking

questions.clue: A researcher samples classrooms from a large district and models variability in baseline achievement across classrooms. How is classroom naturally represented?
choices: An observed residual for each score
A fixed treatment level common to all students
questions.explanation: The classrooms represent a broader population of classroom levels whose variability is of interest.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 354, Random effects

questions.clue: Three treatments are compared on final blood pressure while adjusting for baseline pressure. What role does baseline pressure have?
questions.explanation: The continuous baseline measure enters as an adjustment variable.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 13, Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA)

questions.clue: A table crosses program and completion status. What does a program's row total count?
choices: All people in the entire table
questions.explanation: The row margin adds the counts across all completion categories within that program.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 101, Contingency tables

questions.clue: In a contingency table crossing study mode and pass status, which total belongs in the denominator for the pass probability conditional on studying online?
choices: All students in both study modes
questions.explanation: The condition fixes the online group, so the denominator includes every student in that group.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 101, Contingency tables

questions.clue: Under independence in a contingency table, which information is needed to determine the expected count of a particular cell?
choices: Its observed count and the table total only
All observed counts in its row except its own count
Its row total, its column total and the table total
Its row number and column number
questions.answer: Its row total, its column total and the table total
questions.explanation: The independence model uses the corresponding marginal frequencies to form an expected value.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 156, Expected frequencies

questions.clue: How does Pearson's chi-square statistic combine observed and expected cell counts?
choices: It adds signed discrepancies without weights
It adds expected counts weighted by the observed counts
It adds squared discrepancies weighted by the inverse expected counts
It adds absolute discrepancies weighted by the row totals
It uses only the cell with the largest positive discrepancy
questions.answer: It adds squared discrepancies weighted by the inverse expected counts
questions.explanation: Squaring makes each contribution nonnegative. Dividing by expectation scales the discrepancy for its cell.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 323, Pearson's chi-squared statistic

questions.clue: Which dimensions govern the usual independence-test degrees of freedom for a contingency table with no structural zeros?
choices: The grand total and the smallest cell count
The number of observations and the largest cell count
The number of rows containing a zero count
The numbers of row and column categories
questions.answer: The numbers of row and column categories
questions.explanation: The dimensions determine how many cell counts can vary when the margins are fixed.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 323, Pearson's chi-squared statistic

questions.clue: An independent two-group comparison gives a small 2 by 2 table. Which test conditions on its observed margins to obtain an exact p-value?
questions.explanation: Fisher's test uses the conditional distribution of the cell counts given the margins.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 167, Fisher's exact test

questions.clue: Which pairs supply evidence about the direction of change in the usual McNemar test on before-and-after binary responses?
choices: Pairs that answered yes both times
Pairs that answered no both times
Pairs with different responses at the two times
Pairs whose first response is missing
questions.answer: Pairs with different responses at the two times
questions.explanation: The directional comparison concerns switches from no to yes versus switches from yes to no.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 274, McNemar's test

questions.concept: matched binary measurements across three times
questions.clue: The same participants answer yes or no at three visits. Which standard test compares the three matched response proportions?
questions.explanation: Cochran's Q test extends McNemar's comparison to more than two matched binary measurements.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 88, Cochran's Q-test

questions.clue: In a binary outcome, how do the odds of the event differ from its probability?
choices: Odds compare the event probability to the number of observed trials
Odds express the probability's distance from its median
Odds divide the complement probability by the event probability
Odds compare the event probability to the probability of its complement
Odds always equal the event probability
questions.answer: Odds compare the event probability to the probability of its complement
questions.explanation: Event odds express how likely the event is relative to the alternative that it does not happen.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 309, Odds ratio

questions.clue: Which quantities are compared by a relative risk for exposed and unexposed groups?
choices: Exposure probabilities conditional on the two outcome groups
Event odds conditional on the two exposure groups
Overall event counts regardless of group sizes
The prevalences of the exposure categories
Event probabilities conditional on the two exposure groups
questions.answer: Event probabilities conditional on the two exposure groups
questions.explanation: Risk is the probability of the event within each group, and the relative risk is their ratio.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 364, Relative risk

questions.clue: To form an exposed versus unexposed odds ratio, what two quantities are compared?
choices: The event odds within each exposure group
The event risks within each exposure group
The probabilities of exposure in the full sample
The sizes of the two exposure groups
The numbers of non-events in the groups without denominators
questions.answer: The event odds within each exposure group
questions.explanation: An odds ratio compares event odds, formed within each group before taking the ratio.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 309, Odds ratio

questions.clue: For a binary outcome, what determines whether its logit is positive or negative?
choices: Whether the event has ever been observed in the sample
Whether the two outcome labels are in alphabetical order
Whether the event is more likely or less likely than its complement
Whether the sample size is greater than the event count
Whether the event probability has a finite standard error
questions.answer: Whether the event is more likely or less likely than its complement
questions.explanation: Log odds are positive when the event is more probable than its complement, negative when it is less probable, and zero when both are equally probable.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 258, Logit

questions.clue: What does a binary logistic regression coefficient represent on its original coefficient scale?
choices: The change in probability for a one-unit increase regardless of baseline
The change in the residual standard deviation
The change in log odds for a one-unit predictor increase, holding other predictors fixed
The change in log probability rather than log odds
questions.answer: The change in log odds for a one-unit predictor increase, holding other predictors fixed
questions.explanation: Logistic regression is linear on the log-odds scale. Exponentiating a coefficient gives the odds multiplier.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 257, Logistic regression

questions.clue: A binary regression maps the event probability through the inverse standard normal CDF. Which link is this?
questions.explanation: The probit of a probability is its standard normal quantile.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 340, Probit analysis

questions.clue: Survey responses run from poor to fair to good to excellent. Which model uses that order and imposes a common odds ratio across cutoffs?
questions.explanation: The proportional odds model shares predictor effects across cumulative response thresholds.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 344, Proportional-odds model

questions.clue: Neighbourhood burglary counts are recorded over different numbers of household-years. To model a burglary rate, which offset enters a log-link count model?
questions.explanation: A log exposure offset scales the predicted count in proportion to household-years.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 309, Offset

questions.clue: A route is faster for both peak and off-peak trips. In the combined data, it seems slower because its trips are mostly at peak times. What is the reversal called?
questions.explanation: Combining strata with different weights can reverse comparisons seen in each stratum.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 394, Simpson's paradox

questions.clue: For replicated measurements, residuals centre near zero at both settings. Their estimated standard deviations are 2 at setting A and 7 at setting B. Which assumption does this question?
choices: A zero residual mean across settings
questions.explanation: The two spreads indicate unequal variances despite similar residual centres.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 204, Heteroscedasticity

questions.clue: Residuals are mostly positive at both predictor extremes and negative near the centre. Which problem is most directly suggested?
choices: A fitted intercept that is too large everywhere
A response with constant variance only
questions.explanation: Systematic curvature indicates the linear mean form is missing a pattern.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 367, Residual plots

questions.clue: Residuals over time have long runs of the same sign. Which diagnostic concern is most directly raised?
questions.explanation: Nearby residuals having similar signs is evidence of serial dependence.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 25, Autocorrelation

questions.clue: After adding a predictor strongly aligned with an existing predictor, which quantity is likely to rise for the existing slope, holding the error variance fixed?
questions.explanation: Near redundancy leaves less independent variation to estimate a partial slope.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 287, Multicollinearity

questions.clue: A predictor is regressed on the other predictors in a model. What does an auxiliary R² close to one suggest?
choices: The other predictors almost reconstruct it
The other predictors explain little of it
The target must be measured without error
The original model has constant error variance
The original target is almost uncorrelated with every predictor
questions.answer: The other predictors almost reconstruct it
questions.explanation: A high auxiliary R² means the chosen predictor has little variation left after accounting for the others.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 287, Multicollinearity

questions.clue: A regression includes floor area in both square metres and square feet. What happens if those two columns are exact unit conversions?
choices: The two fitted values must have opposite signs
Each separate slope is always zero
The residual variance must be zero
Their separate standard errors are always one
questions.explanation: Proportional columns carry the same information and make the design rank-deficient.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 287, Multicollinearity

questions.clue: One suspect response is corrected while every predictor value is fixed. What happens to that observation's leverage in the same least-squares model?
choices: It decreases if the response decreases
It increases if the response increases
questions.explanation: Leverage depends on the predictor design and does not depend on the observed response.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 247, Leverage points

questions.clue: An observation lies exactly on the least-squares fitted line and has leverage below one. Why can its Cook's distance indicate no change in the fit after deletion?
choices: Its removal fixes the response mean at zero
Deleting any single observation leaves every least-squares fit unchanged
It has no recorded predictor values
It already agrees exactly with its fitted response
questions.answer: It already agrees exactly with its fitted response
questions.explanation: With a zero residual and no rank loss, deleting the case leaves the fitted coefficients unchanged.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 104, Cook's distance

questions.clue: Which diagnostic directly quantifies how the estimate of one named slope changes when case 18 is omitted?
questions.explanation: DFBETA isolates the change in a particular coefficient when a case is removed.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 132, DFBETA

questions.clue: Two observations have the same raw residual but different estimated residual standard deviations. Which has the larger absolute studentized residual?
choices: The one with smaller raw residual
The residuals are always equal after scaling
The one with the smaller observed response
The one with larger estimated residual standard deviation
The one with smaller estimated residual standard deviation
questions.answer: The one with smaller estimated residual standard deviation
questions.explanation: A studentized residual divides the raw residual by its estimated standard deviation.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 419, Studentized residual

questions.clue: What distinguishes a Pearson residual from a raw residual for a Poisson count?
choices: The discrepancy is converted to an absolute value
The discrepancy is divided by the observed count
The predicted count is added to the observation
The discrepancy is scaled by the square root of the fitted mean
The fitted mean is replaced by the sample maximum
questions.answer: The discrepancy is scaled by the square root of the fitted mean
questions.explanation: A Pearson residual measures the discrepancy in model standard-deviation units.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 323, Pearson's residual

questions.clue: A Poisson count model assumes variance equal to its mean. Across replicates at a fixed predictor value the variance is far larger than the mean. What is this pattern?
questions.explanation: Variation exceeds the Poisson mean–variance assumption.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 314, Overdispersion

questions.clue: In a normal Q–Q plot, residual quantiles lie roughly on a straight line. Which assumption does that visual pattern support?
choices: A linear relation among the predictors
Constant variance at every predictor value
questions.explanation: Agreement between ordered residuals and theoretical normal quantiles supports approximate normality.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 339, Probability plot
